conventions.convention: Gromov product is unnormalized: $(x|y)_o=(d(o,x)+d(o,y)-d(x,y))/2$, with $0\le(x|y)_o\le\min\{d(o,x),d(o,y)\}$; no leading 1/2 factor.

$\delta$-slimness uses closed neighbourhoods defined by infimum point-to-set distance (attainment never assumed), and triangles may be degenerate: repeated vertices and zero-length sides are permitted.

Product constant $\kappa$ is a per-basepoint inequality $(x|z)_o\ge\min\{(x|y)_o,(y|z)_o\}-\kappa$; the four-point condition compares the largest and second-largest opposite-pair sums with gap at most $2\kappa$, ties allowed. The two constants are equal, not halved.

A $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic is any map of a real interval (not assumed continuous or arc-length, one-point domains allowed) with $\lambda\ge1,\varepsilon\ge0$; a $k$-local geodesic is an arc-length path all of whose compact subintervals of length at most $k$ are isometric, and locality statements need $k>0$ (the $k=0$ condition is vacuous).

Hausdorff distance is the maximum of the two one-sided suprema of point-to-set infima, for nonempty sets only; it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ and no finite-valued metric on all subsets and no closest-point attainment is claimed.

Cayley graphs are used as unit-edge geometric realizations (unoriented labelled edges identified with their reversals, loops and parallel edges retained); the standing hyperbolic-group hypothesis is slimness of that specified labelled realization and independence of the generating set is not assumed; the vertex metric is the published $d_S(g,h)=|g^{-1}h|_S$.

Stable translation length is $\tau_S(g)=\lim_{n\to\infty}|g^n|_S/n=\inf_{k\ge1}|g^k|_S/k$; a group is elementary when it is finite or virtually cyclic, and virtually cyclic means having a cyclic subgroup with finitely many left cosets.

Gromov sequences are indexed by positive integers and diverge jointly in both indices (not merely diagonally); equivalence is joint mixed divergence; the boundary product is the supremum over all representative pairs of the double liminf, in $[0,+\infty]$ with no subtraction of infinities, and infinite value is equivalent to equality of classes.

The boundary topology is the one whose open sets are declared by threshold neighbourhoods $U_R(\xi)=\{\eta:B(\xi,\eta)>R\}$ (every point of an open set contains some $U_R$); it is basepoint- and representative-independent, and threshold sets are neighbourhoods but need not be open. The boundary-product inequality costs $3\kappa$.

An isometry is bijective; loxodromic means some basepoint orbit is quasi-isometrically embedded in both directions; poles are the boundary classes of the two signed power sequences; independence means the two pole sets are disjoint; the orbit constants $\tau>0$, $s\ge1$, $C$ of the definition govern all later orbit estimates.

The Morse constant (source convention: product-form hyperbolicity constant) is $M=92\lambda^2(\varepsilon+3\delta)$ with $\delta$ the slimness constant, i.e. $\kappa=3\delta$; the theorem quantifies over possibly discontinuous maps of nonempty compact intervals and over every geodesic with the same endpoints, with no properness.

Dehn presentation convention: $\Delta\ge\max\{3,2\delta\}$, relators are all formal null words of length at most $10\Delta$, spellings need not be freely reduced, and the based shortening is stronger than the cyclic version (which may cross the basepoint and cyclically reduce).

Linear isoperimetry convention: relator lengths at most $L\ge0$ and algebraic area $\operatorname{Area}(w)\le K|w|$ for every null word, measured against the simple realization, with the transfer to the labelled realization costing $12\delta_0(K,L)+8$ and no numerical formula for $\delta_0$ claimed.

AC is assumed only where a statement says so: the Morse projection-family proof, the coarse-inverse selection, the linear-filling converse, the general boundary extension and the proper boundary compactness. The metric equivalences, finite-word arguments, stable length, cone types, pole and coset bounds, north-south dynamics and the tree examples are claimed choice-free; estimates from an already supplied selector are choice-free.

load_bearing.statement: "A geodesic triangle consists of three specified segments joining three points; repeated vertices and zero-length sides are permitted. ... For $\delta\ge0$, a triangle is $\delta$-slim if each side is contained in the closed $\delta$-neighbourhood of the union of the other two sides. ... The Gromov product is $(x|y)_o=\frac{d(o,x)+d(o,y)-d(x,y)}2$. ... For $\kappa\ge0$, the product condition with constant $\kappa$ is $(x|z)_o\ge\min\{(x|y)_o,(y|z)_o\}-\kappa$ for every $o,x,y,z\in X$. ... The four-point condition with constant $\kappa$ says the largest minus the second-largest of these three numbers is at most $2\kappa$, for every quadruple, including repeated points."
"In a geodesic space with $\delta$-slim triangles, $\delta\ge0$, one has $(x|z)_o\ge\min\{(x|y)_o,(y|z)_o\}-3\delta$ for every basepoint $o$ and every $x,y,z$. No properness is required."

"A sequence $x=(x_n)$ is **Gromov** if for every real $R$ there is $N$ such that $(x_n|x_m)_o>R$ whenever $n,m\ge N$. Write $x\sim y$ when for every $R$ some $N$ satisfies $(x_n|y_m)_o>R$ for all $n,m\ge N$. This is joint divergence, not merely diagonal divergence." The boundary product is $(\xi|\eta)_o=\sup\{\liminf_{n,m\to\infty}(x_n|y_m)_o:x\in\xi,\ y\in\eta\}\in[0,+\infty]$.

"In a metric space satisfying the product condition with constant $\kappa\ge0$, mixed-product divergence is an equivalence relation on Gromov sequences. Both being Gromov and this equivalence relation are unchanged by changing the basepoint. In particular this applies to a geodesic $\delta$-slim space with $\kappa=3\delta$, and makes the Gromov-sequence boundary well-defined."

"The **standing hyperbolic-group hypothesis** is that this specified geodesic realization has $\delta$-slim triangles, for some specified $\delta\ge0$ ... Independence of generating set is not assumed here. A group is **elementary** if it is finite or virtually cyclic ... its **stable translation length** in this generating set is $\tau_S(g)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{|g^n|_S}{n}=\inf_{k\ge1}\frac{|g^k|_S}{k}$."

"For $k\ge0$, an arc-length path is **$k$-local geodesic** if each restriction to a compact subinterval of length at most $k$ is an isometric parametrization. ... a **$(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic** is a map $q:I\to X$ ... satisfying $\lambda^{-1}|s-t|-\varepsilon\le d(q(s),q(t))\le\lambda|s-t|+\varepsilon$ for all $s,t\in I$. This does not assume continuity, arc-length parametrization or properness. ... For nonempty subsets $A,B\subseteq X$, their **Hausdorff distance** is $d_H(A,B)=\max\{\sup_{a\in A}d(a,B),\sup_{b\in B}d(b,A)\}$."

"If finite, these satisfy $B_o(\xi,\eta)-2\kappa\le P_o(x,y)\le B_o(\xi,\eta)$. Infinite value for either is equivalent to $\xi=\eta$ ... Moreover $B_o(\xi,\zeta)\ge\min\{B_o(\xi,\eta),B_o(\eta,\zeta)\}-3\kappa$. ... Declare $O$ open when each $\xi\in O$ has some $U_R(\xi)\subseteq O$. This gives a Hausdorff topology, independent of the basepoint and of replacing supremal products by any supplied representative products. Each $U_R(\xi)$ is a neighbourhood, though it need not be open."

"For any metric space and $\kappa\ge0$, the product inequality with constant $\kappa$ at every basepoint is equivalent to the four-point condition whose largest two opposite-pair distance sums differ by at most $2\kappa$. Geodesicity is unnecessary."

"For every infinite-order element $g$ of a finitely generated hyperbolic group, the map $\mathbb Z\to G$, $n\mapsto g^n$, is a quasi-isometric embedding and $\tau_S(g)>0$. This proof is choice-free. In fact there is a positive integer $C$, depending only on the specified Cayley graph and its slimness constant, such that $|g^n|_S\ge|n|/C$ $(n\in\mathbb Z)$, and $\tau_S(g)\ge1/C$."

"In the unit-edge realization of a connected graph with no cycles, there is a unique geodesic between any two points. The three geodesics between any three points form a tripod, allowing legs of length zero. In particular every geodesic triangle is $0$-slim."

"It is **loxodromic** if, for some $o\in X$, there are $\lambda\ge1,c\ge0$ such that $\lambda^{-1}|m-n|-c\le d(g^mo,g^no)\le\lambda|m-n|+c$ $(m,n\in\mathbb Z)$. Its **positive and negative poles** are the boundary classes of $(g^no)_{n\ge1}$ and $(g^{-n}o)_{n\ge1}$. ... Two loxodromics are **independent** when their two pole sets are disjoint. In the standing finitely generated hyperbolic-group setting, every infinite-order element is loxodromic."

"Assume AC for the projection-family proof below. For $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\delta\ge0$, the image of every possibly discontinuous $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic map of a nonempty compact real interval into a geodesic $\delta$-slim space has Hausdorff distance at most $M=92\lambda^2(\varepsilon+3\delta)$ from every geodesic with the same endpoints. No properness is assumed."

"Let $q:[a,b]\to X$ be a $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic in a geodesic metric space, with $a\le b$. If $d(q(a),q(b))\ge2\varepsilon$, there is a continuous $(\lambda,4\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic $p:[a,b]\to X$ with the same endpoints which is $2\lambda$-Lipschitz and satisfies $d(q(t),p(t))\le4\varepsilon$, $d_H(q([a,b]),p([a,b]))\le2\varepsilon$. If instead the endpoint distance is less than $2\varepsilon$, then every image point is within $3\lambda^2\varepsilon+\varepsilon$ of $q(a)$."

"Suppose $q:[a,b]\to X$ is a $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic, $a\le b$, and supplied points $p_a,p_b\in Y$ attain the distances of $q(a),q(b)$ to $Y$. If $d(q(t),Y)\ge D$ for all $t$ and $D\ge15\rho/2+K+\varepsilon/2$, then $d(p_a,p_b)\le2K+8\rho+\max\{5\kappa,4\sqrt2\lambda(b-a)\exp(-\frac{(D-K-\varepsilon/2)\log2}{5\rho})\}$."

concerns.concern: The boundary $\partial X$ is introduced as "the set of equivalence classes of Gromov sequences" while the equivalence relation is only proved in a separate item; that item (`lem-asymptotic-gromov-sequences-form-an-equivalence-relation`) is not named in the body and is not declared as `justified_by`, so the quotient and the supremal boundary product are formally conditional on a later item. The text does say "Once the equivalence relation has been proved", so a reader closes this in seconds, but the declaration convention is worth an explicit adjudication.

Step 2.1 needs the terminal margin $d(x_0,x_n)-t_{n-1}\ge3\delta/2$, i.e. $\operatorname{dist}(x_n,H_{n-1})\ge3\delta/2$ for $H_{n-1}=D(x_n,x_{n-1})$. The cited halfspace-separation lemma displays only $\operatorname{dist}(x_0,D(x_1,x_0))$ and $\operatorname{dist}(x_2,D(x_1,x_2))$ (the two sets that contain the middle point), not the variant with the outer point as the closer one. The missing case is one triangle-inequality line (or the same argument on the reversed geodesic), so the gap closes immediately, but the citation as written does not literally cover it.

Step 4.1 asserts that the infinite class of indices with one fixed value of $b_j=g^{-i(j)N}h^j$ is unbounded and that "step 3.1 gives a later occurrence $j_2>j_1$ with $i(j_2)>i(j_1)$". Existence of such a later occurrence needs the observation that two occurrences with equal $i$ would force $h^{j_2-j_1}=e$, contradicting infinite order (equivalently, $i$ cannot be bounded on an unbounded infinite class while $i(j)\to\infty$). This is reconstructible but not spelled out.

Step 13.1 closes the induction with "Every finite $b-a$ is at most $nh_0$ for some integer $n$" - the Archimedean property of the complete ordered field - which is not among the local real facts assembled in step 1.4/F6; step 14.1 also passes an inequality to the limit $\rho\downarrow\kappa$ without a cited order-passage lemma. Both are elementary and the sister item `def-hg-toolkit-hyperbolic-group-and-stable-length` proves the Archimedean claim inline, so this is polish, but the two passages are the induction's formal entry and exit.

The second paragraph of the Statement says "For a specified geodesic segment $Y=H$, the sharper estimate holds with the additive $2K+8\rho$ term omitted and with $K=0$ in the exponential and distance hypothesis", but does not write the sharper formula; the reader must reconstruct it as $d(p_a,p_b)\le\max\{5\kappa,4\sqrt2\lambda(b-a)\exp(-(D-\varepsilon/2)\log2/(5\rho))\}$ for $D\ge15\rho/2+\varepsilon/2$. Steps 4.1-5.1 do prove that formula, so only the statement's explicitness is at issue.

The B page prose says the examples "do not assert completion of the companion toolkit's open Morse and dynamics theorems". The substantive claim (the five dependency closures avoid `thm-morse-stability-with-explicit-parameter-dependence`, the loxodromic/pole items and the north-south item) holds: the examples use only definitions, the tripod lemma, the free Cayley-tree lemma, the boundary-product topology item and published suppliers. The word "open" describes an authoring state that no longer matches the A page, which now carries full draft proofs of those items.
